note: The row-parity oracle. Each rule is translated to a WHERE clause and run
against the fixture, and evaluated by SEL over the same rows loaded as a
context. The two id lists must match.
This is the only oracle that exercises the `relation` binding, because a
correlated subquery has nothing to correlate to without a query around it.
The closed corpus in expressions.selo covers everything that does not need
a table; this covers what does.
`expect` is not the answer being asserted -- the answer is whatever SEL
says. It is a guard that the fixture still makes the rule discriminate:
the driver fails if a rule selects every order or none, because a rule that

`correlate.raw` is raw SQL by design -- it is the one place a host says something the map cannot know -- and raw SQL does not travel between dialects. So it is written per dialect here, and the driver picks. Backticks are MySQL-family and SQLite; PostgreSQL wants double quotes.
select: SELECT id FROM o WHERE {} ORDER BY id

context.query: SELECT id, credit_limit FROM o ORDER BY id

ITEMS.query: SELECT order_id, qty, price, sku FROM order_items ORDER BY order_id, sku

SKUS.query: SELECT order_id, sku FROM order_items ORDER BY order_id, sku

NOTES.query: SELECT order_id, note FROM order_items ORDER BY order_id, sku

rules.name: sku in the line set
rules.note: SKUS projects one column, so SEL reads it as a list of scalars and IN means the same thing on both sides. IN over the multi-field ITEMS is refused; see the refusal case in sql/cases/09-refusals.sqlt.

rules.name: sku matches, wrong case
rules.degenerate: Empty is the point. The fixture's columns are utf8mb4_general_ci, so a server comparing them under the column collation answers [1] and SEL answers []. This rule is the collation carried into a correlated subquery, which nothing else here checks.
